objectives: Distinguish PWR, BWR, CANDU, fast, MSR designs.
Reason about Gen III+ + Gen IV improvements.

slides.title: Light water reactors: PWR + BWR dominate
slides.body:
**Pressurized Water Reactor (PWR)**:
• Primary loop: water at ~155 bar, ~290-325 °C (subcooled — no bulk boiling).
• Heat transferred to secondary loop via steam generators.
• Secondary loop: steam → turbine → condenser → feedwater pumps → SG. Saturated steam ~70 bar, 285 °C.
• Pressurizer maintains primary pressure via electric heaters + spray.
• Control: control rod insertion (fast) + soluble boron (slow).
• ~62% of global commercial reactors. Designers: Westinghouse, Framatome (France/EDF), Mitsubishi (Japan), KEPCO (South Korea), Rosatom (Russia VVER), CGN/CNNC (China).

**Boiling Water Reactor (BWR)**:
• Single loop: water boils in core at ~70 bar, ~285 °C. Steam goes directly to turbine.
• Steam separator + dryer above core.
• Control: control rods (from below) + recirculation flow.
• Negative void coefficient inherent (steam less moderating than water).
• ~21% of global reactors. Designers: GE, Hitachi-GE, Toshiba.

**Key differences**:
• PWR: simpler containment (secondary loop isolates radioactivity) but more complex (SG, pressurizer). More common globally.
• BWR: simpler core but radioactive primary directly to turbine. Smaller containment.
• Both have decades of operating experience + mature supply chains.

Modern variants:
• **AP1000** (Westinghouse): Gen III+ PWR with passive safety. 4 operating (Vogtle 3+4 US 2023-24; Sanmen + Haiyang China). 1100 MWe.
• **EPR** (Framatome): Gen III+ PWR. 1650 MWe. Olkiluoto Finland, Flamanville France, Taishan China.
• **APR1400** (KEPCO): South Korean PWR exported to UAE.
• **ESBWR** (GE-Hitachi): Gen III+ BWR with passive safety. Licensed but no construction yet.
• **VVER-1200** (Rosatom): Russian Gen III+ PWR; Akkuyu Turkey, Astravets Belarus.

slides.title: CANDU + other moderator/coolant designs
slides.body:
**CANDU (CANada Deuterium Uranium)**:
• Heavy water (D₂O) moderator + coolant in separate channels.
• Natural uranium fuel (no enrichment needed).
• Horizontal pressure tubes — refuelable while running.
• ~7% of global reactors; Canada (Ontario), India, China, Romania, Argentina, South Korea, Pakistan.
• Higher fuel utilization; flexible (can burn natural U, recovered U, thorium, MOX).
• Drawback: D₂O is expensive (~$300/kg vs essentially free H₂O).

**RBMK** (Soviet design): graphite-moderated, water-cooled, channel-type. Chernobyl reactor type. 11 originally built; ~6 still operating in Russia (heavily modified post-Chernobyl).

**Gas-cooled reactors**:
• **Magnox** (UK, 1960s-90s): natural uranium, graphite moderator, CO₂ coolant. All decommissioned.
• **AGR** (UK, 1970s-onwards): advanced gas-cooled, enriched fuel, CO₂. Being phased out.
• **HTGR** (US, Germany, China, Japan): helium coolant, graphite moderator, very high T (~750-950 °C). TRISO fuel inherently safe. China's HTR-PM (Shidao Bay) operating commercially since 2023.

**Fast reactors** (no moderator):
• **Sodium-cooled fast reactor (SFR)**: liquid sodium primary. Russia BN-600, BN-800 (operating). Phenix + Super-Phenix (France, decommissioned). PRISM (US, paper design). Breeder potential (BR > 1) for fuel utilization.
• **Lead-cooled fast reactor (LFR)**: liquid lead/lead-bismuth coolant. BREST-OD-300 (Russia, construction). Westinghouse Lead-Cooled Fast Reactor (US, design).
• **Gas-cooled fast reactor (GFR)**: helium coolant. Mostly conceptual.

Fast reactors enable **closed fuel cycle**: breed Pu-239 from U-238, recycle to fuel. Achieves ~50-100× more energy per kg of natural U than once-through LWR. Used in nuclear-weapons states + countries pursuing fuel-cycle independence.

slides.title: Gen IV + Small Modular Reactors (SMRs)
slides.body:
**Gen IV reactor concepts** (Generation IV International Forum, 2002): goals = improved sustainability, safety, economics, proliferation resistance. Six designs:

1. **Very-High-Temperature Reactor (VHTR)**: HTGR with T > 900 °C; hydrogen production via thermochemical cycles. China HTR-PM operating; Japan HTTR research.
2. **Sodium-cooled Fast Reactor (SFR)**: fast breeder; closed fuel cycle. Russia BN-800; demonstrator program (Japan, France, US TerraPower Natrium).
3. **Supercritical-Water-Cooled Reactor (SCWR)**: water above critical point (374 °C, 22.1 MPa). Higher efficiency. Mostly conceptual.
4. **Gas-cooled Fast Reactor (GFR)**: He-cooled, fast spectrum. Conceptual.
5. **Lead-cooled Fast Reactor (LFR)**: liquid lead. BREST (Russia), Westinghouse.
6. **Molten Salt Reactor (MSR)**: fuel dissolved in molten salt (LiF-BeF₂-UF₄ or chloride salts). Online refueling + reprocessing. ORNL MSRE 1965-69 demonstrated. China TMSR-LF1 (2023 first criticality). US: TerraPower, Kairos, Flibe Energy.

**Small Modular Reactors (SMRs)**: <300 MWe, factory-built modules. Motivations:
• Lower upfront capital ($1-2B vs $10B+ for large LWR) → accessible financing
• Factory production → standardization + manufacturing learning
• Faster construction (3-4 yr vs 5-10+ yr for large)
• Modular: scale by adding units
• Inherent + passive safety: lower decay heat, simpler designs
• Match smaller grids + replacing coal plants 1:1

Leading SMR developers (2024):
• **NuScale Power Module** (US): 77 MWe LWR-style. First US NRC approval (2020); Carbon Free Power Project canceled 2023 over cost.
• **BWRX-300** (GE-Hitachi): 300 MWe BWR. OPG Darlington Canada construction starting 2025.
• **Holtec SMR-300**: PWR-style.
• **Rolls-Royce SMR**: 470 MWe PWR.
• **TerraPower Natrium**: 345 MWe sodium-fast with molten-salt storage.
• **X-energy Xe-100**: 80 MWe HTGR, TRISO fuel.
• **Oklo Aurora**: 1.5 MWe LFR, micro-reactor.
• **Kairos KP-FHR**: 140 MWe fluoride-salt-cooled HTGR (FHR).

Most designs still in licensing or first-of-a-kind construction. Commercial deployment 2025-2035 horizon.

question.question: Compare LWR + CANDU fuel utilization
question.goal: An LWR uses 3.5% enriched U-235 fuel + achieves 50 GWd/t U burnup before refueling. CANDU uses natural U (0.72% U-235) + achieves 7.5 GWd/t U burnup. Compare energy extracted per kg of natural uranium mined.

steps.prompt: Natural U needed per kg of LWR fuel?
hints: 3.5% LEU from 0.72% natural with 0.2-0.3% tails. SWU calculation. Roughly: (feed_U235 - tails_U235) / (product_U235 - tails_U235). With tails 0.25%: 0.0035-0.0025 = 0.001; / 0.0072-0.0025 = 0.0047. So 1 kg LEU needs ~1/(0.001/0.0047) ≈ no, that's wrong. Let me redo: P×x_p + W×x_w = F×x_f, P + W = F → 1 × 0.035 + W × 0.0025 = F × 0.0072. Plus F = 1+W. Solve: 0.035 + 0.0025 W = 0.0072 + 0.0072 W → 0.0278 = 0.0047 W → W = 5.91 kg. So F = 6.91 kg natural U for 1 kg of 3.5% LEU.
steps.reveal: F = 1 + W = 6.91 kg natural U per kg LEU (3.5% with tails at 0.25%).

steps.prompt: Energy per kg of LEU at 50 GWd/t?
hints: 50 GWd × 1 GW/GW × 86400 s/day = 4.32 × 10¹² J/t = 4.32 × 10⁹ J/kg thermal.
steps.reveal: 50 GWd/t × 24 hr/d × 3.6×10¹² J/GWh = 4.32 × 10¹² J/t × (1 t/1000 kg) = 4.32 × 10⁹ J/kg = 1200 MWh/kg thermal.

steps.prompt: Energy per kg natural U for LWR cycle?
steps.reveal: 1200 MWh/kg LEU ÷ 6.91 kg natU/kg LEU ≈ 174 MWh/kg natural U thermal (~58 MWh electrical at 33% efficiency).

steps.prompt: CANDU: 7.5 GWd/t at 0% enrichment. Energy per kg natural U?
steps.reveal: 7.5 GWd/t × 24 hr/d = 180 MWh/kg natural U thermal.

CANDU 180 vs LWR 174 — close, with CANDU slightly ahead. The argument 'CANDU is way better' isn't true for once-through. CANDU's advantages are elsewhere: (1) no enrichment infrastructure needed; (2) on-line refueling enables higher availability; (3) flexible fuel (natural U, thorium, MOX, recovered U); (4) lower fuel cost per kg. But energy per kg natural U is comparable. Closed fuel cycles (fast reactors + reprocessing) extract 50-100× more — the real long-term fuel-utilization advantage.

question.question: Why has the SMR concept attracted both enthusiasm + skepticism?
options: Enthusiasm: factory production should reduce cost via learning + standardization, inherent + passive safety from smaller decay heat, accessible financing (~$1-2B), faster construction (3-4 yr), grid match for distributed power + coal replacement. Skepticism: SMRs lose economy of scale (cost per MWe higher than large LWR), need many units to amortize fixed costs (licensing, supply chain), first-of-a-kind risks (no operating history), regulatory frameworks still adapting, fuel cycle + waste at scale uncertain. NuScale's CFPP cancellation (2023) due to cost overruns was a wake-up call.
All SMRs are identical to existing reactors.
question.explanation:
**SMR case**:

*Pros*:
- Factory production → learning curve, manufacturing efficiency
- Lower upfront capital → fewer parties on hook
- Inherent + passive safety (small decay heat fits passive cooling)
- Faster construction (modular, smaller, less site work)
- Smaller grid + coal-replacement (1 GW coal = 4-12 SMR units)
- Some support cogeneration (district heat, hydrogen)

*Cons*:
- Per-MWe capital cost typically higher (lost economy of scale; capacity factor of LWR-style SMRs lower in some studies)
- Many units needed to amortize fixed costs (licensing, manufacturing line, supply chain, training)
- Regulatory frameworks still adapting (designed for large LWRs)
- First-of-a-kind cost premium
- Fuel cycle + waste handling at scale (1000+ small reactors vs ~400 large) more complex
- Operational staffing per MWe higher
- Cost / risk to first customer high (NuScale CFPP cancellation 2023)

**Market reality (2024)**:
- Many designs, few actually building.
- BWRX-300 (Canada, Ontario Power Generation, construction starting 2025) leading commercial deployment.
- TerraPower Natrium (Wyoming) construction 2024-2030.
- X-energy + Dow chemical partnership (Texas industrial site).
- Rolls-Royce SMR (UK, in licensing).
- Significant government support (Inflation Reduction Act, EU strategic-projects, UK Great British Nuclear, Korea + Japan).

**Open questions**:
- Will factory production deliver promised cost reductions?
- Will regulators streamline licensing for modular designs?
- Will utilities + customers accept first-of-a-kind risk?
- Can deployment ramp fast enough to meaningfully impact decarbonization?

Likely outcome: 10-30 SMRs operating by 2035; meaningful deployment 2030-2050. Large LWRs remain the bulk-power workhorse; SMRs fill niches (small grids, industrial sites, district heat, remote locations).

slides.workedSolution: SMR pros: factory production, lower upfront capex, inherent + passive safety, faster construction, grid match. Cons: per-MWe capex higher (lost economy of scale), need many units to amortize fixed costs, regulatory frameworks adapting, first-of-a-kind risk. NuScale CFPP canceled 2023 over cost. Leading commercial deployments: BWRX-300 (OPG Ontario), TerraPower Natrium (Wyoming), X-energy + Dow. 10-30 units by 2035 likely.

question.question: What makes molten salt reactors (MSR) inherently different from conventional reactors?
options: MSR is the same as PWR.

MSR uses fuel dissolved in molten fluoride or chloride salt as the coolant — fuel + coolant are one fluid. Online refueling + reprocessing possible (fission products extracted continuously); negative temperature coefficient (fluid expands → less fuel in core → less reactivity); operating pressure low (1 atm vs 155 bar PWR); inherent passive safety via freeze plug (gravity drains fuel salt to passively-cooled dump tank); higher operating temperature (~700 °C) enables higher thermal efficiency + hydrogen production; flexible fuel options (U, Th).
Molten salts cannot be used in reactors.
MSR is the same as a fast reactor.
question.explanation:
**Molten Salt Reactor** concept (ORNL MSRE 1965-69; revival 2010s-2020s):

*Fluid fuel*: fissile material dissolved in molten salt (LiF-BeF₂-ZrF₄-UF₄ for MSRE; chloride salts also studied). Operates at ~600-800 °C, ~1 atm.

*Key features*:
- **Fuel + coolant are one fluid**: no fuel cladding, no fuel rods to manufacture, no cladding-failure concern.
- **Online refueling + reprocessing**: continuous extraction of fission products (esp. Xe-135 which boils out; less xenon poisoning); continuous makeup of fissile.
- **Low pressure** (~1 atm vs 155 bar PWR): smaller + cheaper vessel, no high-pressure piping, easier containment.
- **Negative T coefficient**: salt expands → fewer fissile atoms per cm³ → lower k → inherently self-regulating.
- **Freeze plug safety**: at the bottom of the vessel, a salt plug is kept frozen by an electric fan. If power fails, fan stops, plug melts, fuel salt drains into passively-cooled subcritical configuration. **Fail-safe by physics**.
- **High T** (~700 °C) → ~45% thermal efficiency (vs 33% LWR) + hydrogen production via thermochemical cycles.
- **Fuel flexibility**: U-235, U-233 (from Th), plutonium, recycled spent fuel.

*Challenges*:
- Materials: corrosion of structural alloys by molten salt at high T. ORNL Hastelloy-N has track record; modern designs use Ni-based superalloys.
- Tritium: from Li-6 + neutron capture; permeates through alloys → containment design.
- Online reprocessing: requires colocated hot cell or stand-alone facility — adds complexity.
- Licensing: NRC + IAEA frameworks designed for LWRs; MSR-specific licensing in progress.
- No commercial operating fleet → first-of-a-kind risk.

*Active developers*:
- **China TMSR-LF1**: 2 MWth thorium MSR, first criticality 2023 (Gansu). World's first operating MSR since MSRE.
- **TerraPower MSR (TWR)**: previously traveling wave reactor; pivoting to Natrium SFR.
- **Kairos KP-FHR**: salt-cooled (FHR variant, fuel in TRISO not in salt). Construction starting 2024-25 in Tennessee.
- **Flibe Energy**: liquid-fluoride thorium reactor concept.
- **Terrestrial Energy IMSR**: integral MSR for industrial heat + power.
- **Moltex Energy**: stable salt reactor concept.

*Timeline*: commercial MSR likely 2030-2040 horizon. Many designs but few in advanced construction. The TMSR-LF1 milestone (2023 first criticality) is significant first step.

**Why MSR enthusiasts argue**: combines passive safety (inherent physics) + high efficiency + fuel flexibility + waste reduction. **Skeptics**: materials + licensing + reprocessing complexity not yet proven at commercial scale.

slides.workedSolution: MSR has fuel dissolved in molten salt (fluoride or chloride) — fuel + coolant are one fluid. Online refueling + reprocessing; negative T coefficient (expand → less fuel/cm³); low pressure (~1 atm); freeze plug = fail-safe drain to passively-cooled dump tank if power fails; high T (~700 °C) → efficiency; flexible fuel (U, Th). Challenges: corrosion, tritium, reprocessing, licensing, first-of-a-kind. Active developers: TMSR-LF1 (China, first criticality 2023), Kairos, Terrestrial, Moltex. Commercial 2030-2040.

question.question: A 1000 MWe SMR at 95% capacity factor produces how many TWh per year?

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain how Gen IV reactor designs address the weaknesses of Gen II/III LWRs.
question.rubric: Mentions: Gen II/III LWR weaknesses: (1) high pressure → expensive containment; (2) decay heat removal requires active cooling (Fukushima-class risk); (3) limited fuel utilization (1-2% of natural U); (4) waste lasts ~100K yr; (5) low operating T → lower efficiency. Gen IV addresses: (1) lower pressure (MSR ~1 atm; SFR + LFR also low); (2) inherent + passive safety (MSR freeze plug, SFR pool design, gas-cooled reactor inherent shutdown via Doppler); (3) fast spectrum reactors enable closed fuel cycle (50-100× utilization); (4) waste reduced (fission products instead of long-lived actinides); (5) higher T (700-900 °C) → higher efficiency + H₂ production + industrial heat. Concludes that Gen IV is not just incremental — fundamentally different physics + materials + fuel cycles. Timeline: commercial 2030-2050; demonstrator units operating now (BN-800, HTR-PM, TMSR-LF1). Major uncertainties: materials longevity, fuel-cycle infrastructure, licensing, first-of-a-kind cost.
